result: STORM imaging reveals that agrinC forms two distinct layers within the mouse GBM, positioned between podocalyxin-labeled cell membranes. The peak-to-peak distance between agrinC layers is approximately 133-138 nm, and agrin localizes specifically to the GBM rather than to adjacent cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging evidence from STORM imaging, quantitative measurements across hundreds of regions, dual-channel imaging with podocalyxin, and STORM-EM correlation. The consistency between different measurement approaches (80 vs 600+ regions) and validation by multiple imaging modalities strongly supports the two-layer organization of agrinC.

result: Agrin molecules are oriented perpendicular or oblique to the GBM plane with C-termini near cell membranes and N-termini toward the GBM center. AgrinN layers are shifted internally (~8-18 nm) relative to agrinC layers, consistent with agrin's extended conformation and known biochemical interactions.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 combine quantitative STORM measurements of agrinN and agrinC positions with established biochemical knowledge about agrin-laminin interactions and structural data from EM. The observed spatial offset between N- and C-termini is consistent with the ~95 nm extended conformation of agrin, providing strong support for the proposed orientation.

result: Integrin β1 localizes in two layers within the GBM that closely overlap with agrinC layers but are slightly shifted outward toward cell membranes (positions at approximately ±77-80 nm). This spatial relationship is consistent with integrin β1 serving as a cell surface receptor for agrinC.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 and C64-C65 provide quantitative STORM localization data showing integrin β1 distribution overlapping with agrinC, combined with established knowledge that integrin β1 is the major integrin β subunit in these cells and interacts with agrinC. The slight outward shift is biologically plausible for a transmembrane receptor.

result: The N-terminal domains of laminin-521 (LMβ2-LF and LMα5-LEb/L4b) localize to the center of the mouse GBM (approximately -3.2 to -1.8 nm from center), consistent with laminin's cruciform structure having dimensions of 130-150 nm (vertical axis) and 70-80 nm (horizontal axis).
evaluation: Claims C14-C17 and C66 combine quantitative STORM measurements showing central localization of laminin N-terminal domains with established structural knowledge from EM and crystallography. The STORM data are consistent with known laminin dimensions and support a model where laminin short arms meet near the GBM center.

result: Laminin-521 trimers are organized into two separate networks in the mouse GBM, one produced by podocytes and one by endothelial cells, with C-terminal LG domains positioned near the outer aspects (±85-88 nm) and N-terminal domains toward the center. These networks show limited mobility across the GBM thickness.
evaluation: Claims C18-C23 and C68 use transgenic mice with cell-specific expression of human laminin α5 to demonstrate spatial segregation of laminin networks. The STORM data showing LG domains near cells of origin, combined with central localization of N-terminal domains and lack of crossover between networks, provide strong evidence for two distinct laminin networks with limited mobility. This is corroborated by an independent study (C23).

result: Collagen α3α4α5(IV) forms the main collagen IV network in the adult mouse GBM, with both N-terminal (peri-N) and C-terminal (NC1) domains broadly distributed but concentrated near the GBM center (approximately 11-13 nm from center). This collagen isoform is secreted solely by podocytes.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 combine established knowledge about collagen IV structure and assembly with quantitative STORM measurements showing central localization of both termini. The broad distribution with central concentration is consistent with a network architecture, and the podocyte-specific synthesis is supported by citation. The similar positions of N- and C-termini suggest complex network organization.

result: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) localizes specifically to the endothelial side of the adult mouse GBM (center position at -59.5 nm), showing a distinct distribution from collagen α3α4α5(IV). This isoform persists at low levels in the adult GBM and is synthesized by endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C29-C34 combine STORM localization data with established knowledge about collagen IV isoform expression during development. The distinct spatial distributions of the two collagen IV isoforms are clearly demonstrated by STORM, and the endothelial-side localization is consistent with endothelial cell synthesis. The developmental context provides additional support.

result: Nidogen localizes to the center of the mouse GBM (position at -0.22 nm), close to both collagen α3α4α5(IV) and laminin-521 epitopes, consistent with its proposed role as a cross-linker between collagen IV and laminin networks.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 combine quantitative STORM localization data with established biochemical knowledge about nidogen's structure and binding partners. The central localization near both collagen and laminin is consistent with a cross-linking function, though the authors appropriately note limitations in interpreting the exact molecular interactions.

result: The human GBM is approximately twice as thick as the mouse GBM (~428 nm vs ~133-138 nm). This increased thickness is attributed to an expanded collagen α3α4α5(IV) network in the center and an additional layer of laminin-521. Collagen α1α1α2(IV) occupies the space between the central collagen α3α4α5(IV) and the endothelial surface.
evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide comprehensive STORM analysis of human GBM showing integrin β1 peak-to-peak distance of ~428 nm, central localization of collagen α3α4α5(IV), additional central laminin-521 signal not seen in mouse, and distinct spatial organization of the two collagen IV isoforms. The comparative analysis with mouse GBM and consistency across multiple protein markers support the proposed structural differences.

result: In a Col4a3 knockout mouse model of Alport syndrome, the normal two-layer organization of agrinC is disrupted in some GBM segments, and collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution spreads across the GBM width rather than being restricted to the endothelial side. These alterations occur even in segments with relatively preserved agrinC organization, indicating that an intact collagen α3α4α5(IV) network is required to maintain proper GBM organization.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 combine STORM imaging data from Alport model mice with established knowledge about the disease. The segmental disruption of agrinC organization and altered collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution are clearly demonstrated by STORM. The observation that collagen α1α1α2(IV) mislocalization occurs even where agrinC appears organized suggests that collagen α3α4α5(IV) plays a fundamental organizational role.

result: The GBM ECM is a highly structured, laminated assembly where agrin and laminin-521 each form two layers with C-terminal domains near cell membranes and N-terminal domains toward the GBM interior. This organization is consistent with known biochemical interactions between these proteins and cell surface receptors.
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 represent summary conclusions integrating all STORM data with established biochemical knowledge. The consistent orientation of both agrin and laminin molecules, with receptor-binding domains near cells and network-forming domains centrally located, is supported by extensive STORM measurements and aligns with in vitro biochemical studies of protein-protein interactions.

result: The ~200 nm width of the mouse GBM cannot accommodate two fully extended laminin trimers (which would span ~300 nm), suggesting that laminin molecules adopt either a bent conformation or are oriented at an oblique angle relative to adjacent cells.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 present a logical inference from comparing measured GBM thickness with known laminin dimensions. The geometric constraint is clear, and the proposed models (bent or oblique orientation) are reasonable solutions. However, the authors appropriately present this as speculation requiring further investigation, as the STORM data cannot directly distinguish between these models.

result: In human GBM, collagen α3α4α5(IV) N- and C-terminal domains are positioned too far from integrin β1 (~200+ nm separation) for direct ligand-receptor interaction. Instead, agrinC and laminin α5-LG, which localize near integrin β1, are the likely biologically relevant ligands. At the endothelial side, collagen α1α1α2(IV) is positioned close enough to potentially bind integrin β1.
evaluation: Claims C76-C78 draw functional inferences from spatial relationships measured by STORM in human GBM. The large separation between collagen α3α4α5(IV) and integrin β1 makes direct interaction implausible, while the proximity of agrinC and laminin α5-LG to integrin β1 supports their role as ligands. The differential positioning of the two collagen IV isoforms suggests distinct functional roles.

result: Collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers secreted by podocytes permeate through adjacent laminin and agrin networks to concentrate in the GBM center, while collagen α1α1α2(IV) from endothelial cells remains juxtaposed to the endothelium. In Alport syndrome, altered collagen distribution may expose podocytes to unfamiliar collagen IV ligands, potentially contributing to disease pathology.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 combine STORM observations with speculation about molecular mechanisms and disease pathogenesis. While the spatial data showing collagen α3α4α5(IV) in the center despite podocyte-only synthesis is well-supported (C80-C82), the proposed mechanisms of protomer permeation (C81) and the link to Alport pathology (C79, C83) are speculative. These hypotheses are plausible but require experimental validation.

result: A modified Tokuyasu method with 200 nm thick cryosections was optimal for STORM imaging of kidney GBM. The dense protein network in the GBM creates high fluorescence background and light scattering, posing challenges for high-resolution STORM imaging.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 describe methodological optimization and technical challenges. The selection of the Tokuyasu method and 200 nm section thickness is presented as the result of preliminary optimization studies. The observation about fluorescence background and light scattering is a reasonable characterization of the technical challenges encountered.

result: The GBM is composed of ECM proteins (laminin-521, collagen α3α4α5(IV), agrin, nidogen) secreted by flanking podocytes and endothelial cells. These proteins form self-polymerizing networks connected by proteoglycans and nidogen, with some receptors binding directly to ECM proteins. The ~200 nm thickness of mouse GBM is near the diffraction limit of conventional microscopy, and the biological significance of EM-observed lamina densa/lucida is unclear.
evaluation: Claims C52-C63 and C67 represent established background knowledge about GBM composition, protein interactions, and technical limitations of conventional microscopy. These are well-supported by citations and represent the scientific context for the study. The acknowledgment of uncertainty regarding EM observations (C58) is appropriate.
